name: The Life You Can Save (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Moves money: each recipient its donors give to, read live, brings its own countries.
summary: The Life You Can Save recommends about thirty charities fighting extreme poverty and raises money for them, through its own giving channels in the US and Australia and by influencing gifts made to the charities directly; this model covers both entities' work in 2025 ($2.6M of operating costs). At the defaults it averts about 13 years of healthy life per $1,000: of the $24.3M it reports moving (with unreported influenced gifts allowed for and Founders Pledge's share of the emergency fund they ran together taken out), the site's shared figure for a meta charity without a donor survey says it caused 30%, about $7.3M or nearly three dollars per dollar it spends, each dollar valued where its money went (its own split by charity, each charity at its figure on the rankings), half counted as new money, after a short wait for its grants, and the next dollar at 28% of the 2025 average. The result moves most with its next-dollar figure, the share of the giving it caused and credit by share of resources; 18 of its 33 recipient charities and its emergency fund (53% of the money) have no model here and are valued at the average of the rest. No branch is discounted for missing data, since money moved is counted.

rows.explainer: The Life You Can Save US and Australia together, as the charity itself aggregates them in its annual report ($2,617,394 there, at its own exchange rate). Grants passed on to charities are excluded: they are the money moved, not spending on moving it.

rows.label: Operating expenses on the programme (all of them)
rows.explainer: The Life You Can Save has one programme: recommending charities (research and evaluation) and getting people to give to them (outreach, the book, workplace and online giving, donor services, the US and Australian giving channels). Its management and its fundraising serve that programme, which is itself fundraising for other charities, so all operating expenses are programme cost and the overhead multiplier is 1. The Form 990's split (most of the US cost under fundraising) doesn't change the total cost of the money moved.

rows.label: Spending on the modelled programme in 2025 (raising money for its recommended charities)
rows.explainer: The whole operating budget of both entities in calendar 2025, the latest year with both a filed Form 990 and a published money-moved report. No part of the work is left out: every activity aims at the money moved. The US accounts are audited (the 990's Schedule D, Part XII, reconciles to the audited financial statements); the statements themselves are not posted, so the 990 (filed October 2026) and the charity's 2025 financials summary are the sources.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programs in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.label: Influenced gifts actually made, per dollar reported (charities', donors' and intermediaries' reports)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The three reported channels count only gifts someone told the charity about: by its own account only about half its recommended charities report any, fewer than 100 donors reported theirs, and some giving platforms have no tracking. If the non-reporting charities received half as much influenced money per charity as the reporting ones, the true total would be about 1.5 times the reported one; we take 1.25 because the charities that report are likely the ones with the most such gifts. Low 0.9: only what was reported, less some overlap, since the source doesn't say a gift reported by both the charity and the donor is counted once. High 2: as much again unreported. This is about counting the gifts, not whether they were caused by the charity: that is the own-effect question (donor_own_effect).

source.title: The Life You Can Save, Money Moved 2025: By Charity

rows.explainer: The emergency fund it ran with Founders Pledge after the 2025 aid cuts ($13.1 million in all, by its annual report); this is the part it counts as its own money moved.

rows.label: Its share of the credit for the Rapid Response Fund money it counts
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The fund was a joint campaign with Founders Pledge (and Project Resource Optimization), whose own outreach and grant-making stand behind the same gifts (Convention 2: credit is the charity's share of the resources behind the outcome). The $3.1 million it counts is the part given through its own channels, so it keeps most of the credit: 75%, from an even split with Founders Pledge (50%) to all of it (100%). Only this co-run fund is shared; the other channels are its own outreach.

rows.label: Money moved credited to it before its own effect, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: All channels less the part of the Rapid Response Fund credited to Founders Pledge, its partner in running the fund.

rows.label: Share of these donations The Life You Can Save caused (its own effect)
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure for a meta charity with no donor survey of its own: 30% (15% to 45%), from Giving What We Can's donor surveys. The Life You Can Save publishes no survey of what its donors would have given without it; many give through it because it passes their gifts on tax-deductibly, or would have found its charities anyway. The rest of the recorded giving would have gone to the same charities without it. Whether the gifts it caused are new money or shifted from other charities is the separate new-money question below.

rows.label: Money moved that The Life You Can Save caused, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: Recorded money moved, credited, times its own effect. Valued only through the shared rows below: whether the money would otherwise have been given at all is the site's one new-money share, where it goes is the charity's own published split, and the next dollar against this year's average is its own next-dollar figure. No leverage ratio or counterfactual share of the charity's own is used.

rows.label: Money moved it caused per dollar of its cost
rows.explainer: Context, and the donors' share of the resources with credit by share of resources on.

rows.label: Average time a gift through its accounts waits before it reaches the charity (years)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: gifts to The Life You Can Save are designated to a named charity and passed on as agency funds, so most wait weeks to a few months. The US entity's liabilities at the end of 2025, $3,385,374 (Form 990 Part X line 26, nearly all of it one line, $3,242,438, money held for the charities or grants payable), over the $10.0M it granted that year give 0.33 years, the high end: December's giving peak inflates the year-end balance. 0.15 years (0.05 to 0.33).

Side effects of the money moved, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: Good and harm beyond the donations counted: gifts to its charities by people who read Peter Singer's book The Life You Can Save, its podcast or its recommendations and never tell anyone (beyond the unreported gifts already allowed for in reach), and a wider norm of giving to the poorest that it argues for in public (positive); donor attention drawn from other good uses, and gifts it steers to charities that do less than the ones donors would otherwise have chosen (negative). 5% (−5% to +20%) of the modelled value, our judgment, the figure our models of Giving What We Can and Effektiv Spenden use for the same kind of effects.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to The Life You Can Save's recommended charities (its 2025 split, live), units of value
rows.explainer: The Life You Can Save's own published split of the money it moved in 2025, by charity, each charity at its figure on the rankings under your values (its programmes and locations weighted by funding; Evidence Action, for one: syphilis screening, iron and folic acid, deworming, in-line chlorination and Dispensers for Safe Water); a charity with no figure on the rankings (Raising the Village) at its model; Carbon180 and Evergreen Collaborative, climate charities without a model, at Clean Air Task Force's, the one climate recipient modelled. The 13 charities with a model here took $11.3 million of the $24.1 million; the rest (18 charities and its Rapid Response Fund, none modelled here) is valued at the average of these, so it drops out of the mix.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: Valued by where this organisation's money actually went: its own published split by charity, each at its live result on this site.

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.label: Value of the money moved (units of value)
rows.explainer: Money moved it caused, after the wait for its grants, at the net value of a dollar moved (shared rows), plus its side effects.

Donated services and use of facilities received by the US entity in 2025

source.title: The Life You Can Save, Form 990 for 2025 (public disclosure copy)
source.page: Schedule D, Part XII (reconciliation of expenses per audited financial statements), line 2d and Part XIII

rows.explainer: Others' resources behind the same money moved: the audited statements count $250,000 of donated services (total expenses per audited statements $2,436,517 against $2,186,517 on the 990). By Convention 2 it stays out of the cost and lowers the charity's share of credit instead. The Australian entity publishes no in-kind figure.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Applies to the policy branch only, which is 0 here; the money moved has its own steps (own effect, new money, destinations). Kept at the template's figure.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Applies to the policy branch only, which is 0 here; the money moved has its own steps (own effect, new money, destinations). Kept at the template's figure.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the money moved: its own operating cost against that cost plus the donated services it received (Convention 2), 91%. The Rapid Response Fund's co-run credit is taken in the reach section. Applied to the money moved as well as to the (zero) policy branch.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Missing-data discount
rows.explainer: The site's missing-data discount (Convention 12) for the empty policy branch. The money moved is counted dollars (its accounts' grants and the gifts reported to it), so it takes no missing-data step; each destination read live brings its own.

rows.label: Total adjustment (policy branch)
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above, for the policy branch.

rows.label: Total value (units of value)
rows.explainer: The value of the money moved, times the charity's share of the resources behind it (the donated services it received); the policy and career branches are 0. The other adjustments stay with the policy branch, so nothing is counted twice.

rows.label: Value per dollar
rows.explainer: The outcome per dollar of its 2025 operating cost, in units of value.

rows.explainer: Staff pay of the US entity, whose operating cost is 84% of the two entities'; it is 82% of the US operating cost (staff_cost_share below).

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of operating cost
rows.explainer: From its own Form 990: US salaries and benefits over US operating expenses (82%); the Australian entity, with no functional split published, is assumed to be the same. rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: The shared pay gap for researchers, advisers and policy staff (@staff_pay.gap_research_policy): its staff evaluate charities and run outreach and donor services, closer to an evaluator's or adviser's job than to campaigning or media.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar of 2025
rows.explainer: The Life You Can Save's own figure (facts/next_dollar.json, docs/normalization.md 2.10): 28% (13–63%). This model is its 2025 spending over everything that spending moved; the extra operating cost from 2024 to 2025 came with about half the money moved per dollar of the year's average, part of 2025's money moved was a one-off emergency fund, and the two entities hold about 22 months of their operating costs in reserve, most of it in Australia.
